A nature-inspired, research-grounded 2D educational game for Mars-colony decision making

What if the key to designing a sustainable Mars habitat were hidden in a honeycomb?

Players become fictional space bees, explore an abandoned Martian greenhouse, collect honey as symbolic credits, manage oxygen and dust-storm hazards, and invest in bases and a Zinnia Zone. The game is developed in GDevelop using visual events, with multiple scenes and local device saves. No accounts or remote server are required.

NASA REFERENCE VALUE

DOCUMENTED FACT

WHY IT MATTERS FOR THE GAME

Atmospheric pressure

Approx. 6.36 mbar at mean radius; varies by season [1]

A sealed, controlled base is necessary; oxygen in-game is a simplified survival mechanic.

Mean temperature

Approx. 214 K (−59 °C) [1]

Greenhouse and habitat protection are meaningful design choices.

Surface gravity

Approx. 3.73 m/s² (0.38 × Earth) [1]

Distinguishes Martian conditions from Earth and ISS microgravity.

Solar irradiance

Approx. 586 W/m² at Mars vs 1,361 W/m² at Earth [1]

Energy is limited; dust may further reduce solar effectiveness [3].

 

Research based on data.nasa.gov

We reviewed NASA Open Data Portal entries at data.nasa.gov and linked each dataset to an educational scenario. The catalog describes archived NASA observations and points to Planetary Data System collections. At the time checked, the selected portal entries displayed “This dataset has no data” in the on-page resources panel; therefore, this report does not claim that raw files were downloaded, analyzed, or integrated into the game. [4–7]

NASA OPEN DATA RECORD

WHAT THE RECORD CONTAINS

ROLE IN SPACE BEES / STATUS

MGS atmospheric temperature-pressure profiles [4]

Over 21,000 atmosphere profiles from Mars Global Surveyor radio occultations.

Scientific basis for a hostile atmosphere; reference-only at present.

Phoenix meteorological pressure / temperature [5]

Calibrated temperature and pressure observations, including 2-second sampling and 512-second averages.

Supports the concept of weather-dependent decisions; no numerical in-game import.

MER Pancam atmospheric opacity [6]

Atmospheric opacity values derived from the rovers’ panoramic cameras.

Evidence that airborne dust can be studied quantitatively; supports dust-storm concept.

Viking lander daily average pressure [7]

Sol-by-sol average surface-pressure series and summary statistics.

Example of time-varying Martian conditions; possible future offline scenario dataset.

 

RECENT NASA RESEARCH (2026)

NASA’s Science Data Portal described ongoing work on a Martian atmosphere foundation model in June 2026, updated August 2026. The article highlights sparse and fragmented measurements and the challenge of modeling dust opacity. This reinforces our decision to present storms as educational scenarios—not as reliable forecasts. [10]

Data-informed expansion proposed (not yet implemented)

•  Choose a traceable NASA archive and document its units, time range and instrument.

•  Extract or manually transcribe a small, permitted set of measurements; check missing values.

•  Convert measured values to transparent difficulty categories (e.g., clear / dusty), with defined thresholds.

•  Bundle the resulting scenario table locally so the game remains account-free and offline; show the dataset citation in the game.

 

03  |  GAMEPLAY, SCIENCE & THE BEE CONCEPT

A mission with meaningful decisions

The player is a space bee assigned to scout an abandoned greenhouse on Mars. In every mission, the bee gathers honey credits, watches oxygen, reacts to environmental threats and returns to the colony. Credits can be spent on building and upgrading bases and expanding the Zinnia Zone. Progress therefore depends not only on collection, but also on prioritization. The game is a science-communication tool, not a validated engineering simulation.

PLAYER STEP

GAME ACTION

EDUCATIONAL OUTCOME

EXPLORE

Move through 2D scenes and enter a greenhouse area.

Notice the need for protected growing environments.

COLLECT

Gather honey as symbolic in-game currency.

Identify scarcity, effort and opportunity cost.

ASSESS

Monitor oxygen and approaching dust-storm warnings.

Practice risk assessment and returning to shelter.

INVEST

Spend credits on colony bases and Zinnia Zone upgrades.

Compare short-term rewards with long-term resilience.

REPEAT

Use the updated colony to plan the next mission.

Understand feedback loops and connected systems.

 

Why honeybees and hexagons?

Honeybees demonstrate organized cooperation, efficient use of space and connected hexagonal comb structures. Our modular-colony aesthetic uses these principles as biomimicry and storytelling. We are not proposing to transport real bees to Mars, nor claiming that hexagons alone make a Mars habitat structurally safe.

Zinnia Zone: a documented NASA connection

NASA reported that a zinnia bloomed in the International Space Station’s Veggie facility on 16 January 2016, following an experiment begun in November 2015. The experiment addressed the challenges of growing flowering plants in microgravity. In the game, Zinnia Zone is a protected growing area inspired by this research. ISS microgravity and Mars surface gravity are different; this is conceptual inspiration, not proof that flowers can grow outdoors on Mars. [8–9]

WHAT IS REAL, WHAT IS FICTIONAL?

FACT: Martian environmental constraints and ISS zinnia research are real NASA topics. GAME DESIGN: space bees, honey credits, oxygen bars and storm alerts simplify those topics. FUTURE WORK: any measured NASA data driving a game parameter must be separately implemented and validated.

 

 

04  |  HOW THE STUDENT BUILT THE PROJECT

Technical implementation

The student reports building the game as a 2D, multi-scene project with GDevelop. No traditional programming language was handwritten: the game logic was configured through GDevelop’s visual condition/action event system. Progress is saved locally on the device, with no server connection or player account. GDevelop’s official documentation supports the event-editor and local-storage capabilities. [11–12]

Development workflow

•  Research: define the Mars-habitat problem and read NASA scientific sources.

•  Concept: choose honeybees, hexagonal modularity, missions and the Zinnia Zone.

•  Implementation: create scenes and configure interactions in GDevelop visual events.

•  Game systems: connect collection to spending and environmental decisions.

•  Persistence: store save information locally; avoid a sign-in requirement.

•  Documentation: cite each NASA fact, separate science from fiction and prepare a demonstrable prototype.

VERIFICATION BOUNDARY

Implementation details are based on the student’s verbal description and team presentation, not on an independent code, scene or gameplay inspection. The specific storage keys, algorithms, storm thresholds and game asset licenses must be confirmed in the project files before final submission.

 

 

05  |  ORIGINALITY, FEASIBILITY & POTENTIAL IMPACT

Why the project deserves attention

SPACE BEES connects three areas that are rarely taught together in one short game experience: bee-inspired design, NASA planetary and space-biology research, and resource-management gameplay. Its primary innovation is an educational combination and interactive framing—not a claim to have discovered a new Martian habitat technology.

PROJECT STRENGTH

Accessible science and sustainability education for younger learners.

A short classroom pilot and clear learning goals.

Suggested evaluation (not yet reported as completed)

•  Usability: ask 5–10 students to play one mission; record whether they can collect, return and spend without assistance.

•  Learning: give three short questions about Martian air, dust and controlled agriculture before and after play.

•  Balance: measure oxygen-related mission failures and whether storm warnings are understandable.

•  Reliability: test save, exit, reopen and resume on the intended device.

•  Evidence: retain screenshots of the NASA-source references and game scenes, plus short notes on what changed after feedback.

Budget-management analogy

Honey is a fictional currency, not real money or a physical commodity on Mars. To show why prioritizing limited budgets matters, Rocket Lab reported average revenue per launch of US$8.7 million for the nine months ended 30 September 2026. This is a transaction-price / revenue metric, not the cost of building a rocket and not a universal market price. The game does not model actual launch finances. [13]

 

06  |  SUBMISSION-READY TEXT & NEXT ACTIONS

Copy-ready project submission

Project title and short pitch

SPACE BEES: Mars Colony — A Biomimicry-Based Educational Game

SHORT PITCH

What if a beehive could inspire the way we learn to live on Mars? SPACE BEES is a GDevelop-made 2D game in which fictional space bees collect symbolic resources, navigate oxygen and dust hazards, and invest in modular colony bases and a Zinnia Zone inspired by NASA’s ISS plant research.

 

Project description for the NASA Space Apps page

SPACE BEES: Mars Colony is an educational 2D resource-management game created to make the challenges of a future Mars settlement understandable to young learners. Inspired by honeybee cooperation and hexagonal honeycomb structures, players explore a Martian greenhouse, collect honey credits, monitor oxygen, respond to dust-storm warnings and reinvest resources in colony development and a protected Zinnia Zone. The project combines NASA-documented Martian environmental facts with the ISS Veggie zinnia experiment and cataloged Mars atmospheric datasets found through NASA Open Data Portal. The student developed the multi-scene prototype in GDevelop using visual events, without handwritten programming code. Save data remain local; no account or server is required. NASA sources currently inform the project’s research and educational scenarios; live NASA dataset integration has not been implemented. Future work will add traceable offline data-driven scenarios and evaluate student learning with short pre/post activities. The project invites a simple but powerful question: can lessons from nature help us make smarter choices for life beyond Earth?

Source numbers support the stated facts. No retrieved NASA atmospheric measurements have been numerically incorporated into the current game; the stated use is literature and dataset-catalog research. Game features and technical implementation are the student’s description and should be demonstrated in the actual build.

 

FINAL MESSAGE  •  We did not just imagine life on Mars. We connected that imagination with credible science, purposeful choices and a student-built game.
